title: Is the Eyring Plot Misleading? A Case for Arrhenius Analysis of Activation Parameters
abstract: A common view in physical chemistry literature is that the Eyring representation, in which a linear fit of $\ln(k/T)$ versus $1/T$ is attempted, is more fundamental than the Arrhenius representation, $\ln(k)$ versus $1/T$. This perception is typically motivated by its derivation from statistical mechanics and quantum mechanics, and by the interpretation of the intercept in terms of the activation entropy $ΔS^\ddagger$, whereas the Arrhenius equation and its prefactor are often regarded as purely phenomenological. However, harmonic approximation models yield exact linearity in Arrhenius plots but not in Eyring plots, although for real experimental data both generally appear equally linear within typical experimental accuracy. Furthermore, the impression that the Eyring formulation is inherently quantum mechanical arises from the presence of the Planck constant in the prefactor, whereas this term results from normalization conventions in the partition function. This also highlights an interpretational issue in $ΔG^\ddagger$, which is based on partition functions of different dimensionality between reactant and transition state. This dimensional mismatch can be reformulated in an alternative representation that improves interpretability and reduces to an Arrhenius-type expression in which the prefactor is directly related to an entropy of activation. In this framework, both activation enthalpy and entropy obtained from an Arrhenius fit are arguably more physically relevant than the corresponding Eyring fit values.
summary: This paper critically examines whether the Eyring or Arrhenius formulation is more fundamentally correct for describing reaction rates. By analyzing theoretical derivations from TST using harmonic and hard-core potentials, the author argues that an Arrhenius analysis yields parameters ($\Delta H^\ddagger, \Delta S^\ddagger$) that are more physically consistent than those derived from the standard Eyring plot due to underlying mathematical inconsistencies.
main_problem: The paper debates the relative fundamental nature of the Eyring representation versus the Arrhenius representation for calculating chemical reaction rate constants from temperature-dependent measurements.
main_result: The author argues that activation enthalpies and entropies derived from an Arrhenius fit are arguably more physically relevant than those obtained directly from the standard Eyring plot analysis due to inherent dimensional mismatches in the free energy of activation ($\Delta G^\ddagger$).
method: The analysis compares rate expressions derived from Transition State Theory (TST), contrasting harmonic approximation results with derivations using reactive flux formalism and proposing a modified potential restraint approach.
model_or_system: The study models chemical reactions using TST, comparing the standard Eyring equation ($k \propto e^{- eta \Delta G^\ddagger}$) against the Arrhenius form ($k \propto e^{ eta E_a}$). It utilizes harmonic and hard-core potential approximations to analyze the temperature dependence of activation parameters.
key_observables: Rate constant ($k$), Activation Enthalpy ($\Delta H^\ddagger$), Activation Entropy ($\Delta S^\ddagger$), Gibbs Free Energy of Activation ($\Delta G^\ddagger$).
important_parameters: Temperature ($T$), Planck's constant ($h$), Boltzmann constant ($k_B$), and various potential energy surface parameters.
main_assumptions: The analysis relies on harmonic approximations for potentials, assumes the validity of TST derivations, and proposes modifications (like using an infinite square-well restraint) to improve parameter consistency.
figures_summary: Figure S1 illustrates a particle confined in a water slab between two membranes, representing a hard-core system used in model calculations.
paper_structure: The paper progresses by first establishing the conflict between Eyring and Arrhenius interpretations; it then details derivations using classical statistical mechanics and reactive flux expressions; finally, it proposes an alternative framework using modified potential restraints to yield consistent Arrhenius parameters.
why_interesting: While focused on chemical kinetics, the rigorous comparison of different theoretical frameworks (Eyring vs. Arrhenius) for extracting fundamental thermodynamic quantities ($\Delta H^\ddagger, \Delta S^\ddagger$) is highly relevant to understanding approximations and limitations in statistical mechanical models used across AMO physics.
